summary: A status report that identifies the documents specifying the official protocols used in the Internet, with comments on planned revisions or changes. It replaces RFC 991 and has since been updated by later RFCs.

eli5.summary: It is a reading list of the rulebooks the Internet officially followed in 1987, with notes about what was expected to change.

subtitle: A May 1987 checklist of which documents define the Internet's protocols, and how required each one was.

tldr.problem: By 1987 the Internet's protocols were scattered across many RFCs, handbooks and other documents, and implementers needed to know which ones counted as official.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 1011 is an outline with one entry per protocol. Each entry gives a status (required, recommended, elective, experimental or none), the defining specification, comments on known problems, other references, dependencies and a contact.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 991 and its predecessors as the status report of May 1987, and it was itself later updated by RFC 6093 and RFC 9293. It is a snapshot of 1987, not a current list.

today: RFC 1011 replaced RFC 991 and was itself later updated by RFC 6093 and RFC 9293; its status is recorded as Unknown. It describes which protocols were official in May 1987 and should be read as a historical snapshot.

sections.title: What the Memo Is For
sections.content:
RFC 1011 is an official status report on the protocols used in the Internet community. It identifies the documents that specify the official protocols and notes any revisions or changes planned. It obsoletes RFC 991 along with RFCs 961, 943, 924, 901, 880 and 840.

To first order, the official protocols are those in the DDN Protocol Handbook (DPH) of December 1985, a three-volume set about 5 inches thick. The memo also names older collections, such as the Internet Protocol Transition Workbook of March 1982 and the ARPANET Protocol Handbook of January 1978, and says nearly all their relevant material was reproduced in the DPH.
sections.eli5: It is a list that points to the books where each Internet rule is written down, so nobody has to guess which book to open.

sections.title: The Status Levels
sections.content:
Each entry in the outline has notes on status, specification, comments, other references, dependencies and contact. The status is one of five values, and the memo defines what each asks of a host.

  • required: all hosts must implement the protocol.
  • recommended: all hosts are encouraged to implement it.
  • elective: hosts may implement it or not.
  • experimental: hosts should not implement it unless they are taking part in the experiment and have coordinated with the contact person.
  • none: this is not a protocol.
sections.eli5: Some rules are like brushing your teeth: everyone must. Some are like eating vegetables: please do. Some are optional, some are science projects, and some are not rules at all.

sections.title: How the Outline Is Organized
sections.content:
The outline starts with an overview entry, the Catenet Model (IEN 48), which has status none and gives an overview of the organization and principles of the Internet. It then groups protocols into network level, host level and application level, followed by appendices.

The network level lists the Internet Protocol (IP, RFC 791) and the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP, RFC 792), both required, and the Internet Group Multicast Protocol (IGMP), which is recommended. The host level includes UDP and TCP (both recommended), EGP (recommended for gateways) and several experimental protocols. The application level covers Telnet, FTP, SMTP, the Domain Name Protocol and many smaller services, with statuses ranging from recommended to experimental.
sections.eli5: The list is sorted like a school: first the rules for the building (network), then for each classroom (host), then for the games you play in it (applications).

sections.title: Known Problems in Core Specifications
sections.content:
The comments in each entry record known problems with the specification. For IP, the memo points out confusion in the route options: the pointer begins at 4. It says ICMP is an integral part of IP, so an implementation is not complete without it, and that the subnet procedures of RFC 950 are an essential part of the IP architecture that must be implemented by all hosts and gateways.

For TCP, the comments list clarifications still needed. The urgent pointer points to the last octet of urgent data. Idle connections are fine and should not be closed, and no TCP probe mechanism is needed. Segments that arrive out of order may be kept, and not keeping them carries a very large performance penalty. If the user time out fires, the user should be notified, but the connection should not be closed.

The TCP Maximum Segment Size is the IP Maximum Datagram Size minus forty. The default IP datagram size is 576, so the default TCP segment size is 536 (see RFC 879).
sections.eli5: The list also has sticky notes on the pages: here is a typo, here is a part people misread, and here is what it really means.

sections.title: Appendices and Other Standards
sections.content:
The appendices point to supporting documents rather than protocols. Assigned Numbers (RFC 1010, issued May 1987) lists the protocol field values currently assigned. Pre-emption (RFC 794) is elective and describes how to pre-empt TCP connections. Service Mappings and Address Mappings are marked out of date and in need of revision.

The memo ends with entries for related standards from outside the Internet community, such as the ISO Transport Protocol specification (RFC 905), ISO transport services on top of TCP (RFC 1006) and the mapping between X.400 and RFC 822 mail (RFC 987). These entries carry no status value.
sections.eli5: At the back there are extra pages: a phone book of assigned numbers and notes about how Internet rules fit with rules from other groups.
